**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Block split recursive rm flags**

When Codex evaluates `rm -r -f build` or `rm -f -r build`, neither command matches this two-token pattern, so it falls back to the normal approval policy despite having the same recursive-force behavior the justification says is never delegated. Codex requires an exact prefix match for a rule's pattern ([Rules documentation](https://developers.openai.com/codex/rules)); add explicit rules and inline match tests for the separated-flag forms (and any other intended spellings).

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Restart Codex after replacing its rules**

For an already-running Codex session, this update does not activate the new denies: Codex scans rule files at startup and its rules documentation explicitly requires a restart, while `make update` only replaces the file and reloads Herdr. A resident worker therefore continues using the policy it loaded before `chezmoi apply` until it exits or is restarted. Restart the relevant Codex sessions as part of applying this policy, or document that activation step. [Rules documentation](https://developers.openai.com/codex/rules)

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L78-L78](https://github.com/mryfmo/dotfiles/blob/a0b059059485904fc221a02277b50e437cd713ed/AGENTS.md#L78-L78)

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Prevent make targets from bypassing chezmoi apply**

When an agent runs `make update` or `make apply`, the exec request begins with `make`, so this prefix rule does not match; the target then runs `chezmoi apply --verbose` as a subprocess (`Makefile:63`). Execpolicy matches the argument list supplied to Codex rather than spawned subprocesses ([Rules documentation](https://developers.openai.com/codex/rules)), so an approved external `make update` performs the operator-only apply despite this rule. Deny those make targets too, or move the apply behind an operator-only entry point.

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L78-L78](https://github.com/mryfmo/dotfiles/blob/a0b059059485904fc221a02277b50e437cd713ed/AGENTS.md#L78-L78)

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Cover alternate chezmoi apply entry points**

A worker can bypass this fixed-second-token rule with `chezmoi init --apply`: `make init` already invokes exactly that form at `Makefile:34-35`, and `--apply` runs `chezmoi apply` according to the [chezmoi init documentation](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/commands/init/). The same pattern also misses the private-domain apply form already used at `Makefile:65-67` (`chezmoi --source … --config … apply`), so either public or private dotfiles can still be applied directly despite the documented operator-only policy. Add forbids for these entry points, or narrow the documented guarantee.

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L78-L78](https://github.com/mryfmo/dotfiles/blob/04d6e1f3df8a454bc01334cef463b1a77e1cf4f6/AGENTS.md#L78-L78)

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
items.disposition: not-applicable:the `chezmoi --source <d> --config <f> apply` form has an arbitrary-valued global option before the subcommand, which a prefix rule cannot match without forbidding all of chezmoi machine-wide (blocking chezmoi diff/status); chezmoi init --apply and make init were fixed in e16012eb and chezmoi init/edit are now forbidden wholesale (c58e4835); documented as outside prefix coverage in 7a7c21cd, the sandbox is the backstop (PONG decision 1, option c)

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Cover combined rm force/recursive flags**

`rm -rfv build` (and reordered forms such as `rm -vrf build`) is a valid GNU `rm` invocation containing recursive, force, and verbose options, but it does not equal any of the second-token alternatives here and therefore falls through to the normal approval policy. GNU documents the recursive and verbose options in its [rm invocation reference](https://www.gnu.org/s/coreutils/manual/html_node/rm-invocation.html); add the combined variants and matching tests so the stated never-delegate rule is not bypassed by a common verbose form.

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L78-L78](https://github.com/mryfmo/dotfiles/blob/04d6e1f3df8a454bc01334cef463b1a77e1cf4f6/AGENTS.md#L78-L78)

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Block Terraform applies with global options**

Terraform documents `-chdir` as a global option that appears before the subcommand, including `terraform -chdir=environments/production apply`. Because this pattern requires `apply` to be the second token, `terraform -chdir=environments/production apply -auto-approve` falls through to the normal approval policy and can modify infrastructure whenever a worker targets another module directory. Add coverage for the global-option form (and a matching test) so the operator-only infrastructure guarantee holds. [Terraform CLI documentation](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands)

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L78-L78](https://github.com/mryfmo/dotfiles/blob/04d6e1f3df8a454bc01334cef463b1a77e1cf4f6/AGENTS.md#L78-L78)

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Block the absolute sudo path**

On macOS, this repository itself uses `/usr/bin/sudo` in `setup.sh:142-150`, but this rule matches only the literal first token `sudo`. An agent can therefore invoke `/usr/bin/sudo …`, which falls through to the ordinary approval policy and permits the privilege escalation that this rule says is never delegated. Include the supported absolute path in the forbidden alternatives and add a match test for it.

AGENTS.md reference: [AGENTS.md:L78-L78](https://github.com/mryfmo/dotfiles/blob/04d6e1f3df8a454bc01334cef463b1a77e1cf4f6/AGENTS.md#L78-L78)

`setup` is absent from this union, so `make setup` receives the normal policy even though its recipe invokes `./setup.sh`; that wrapper reaches `chezmoi apply` at `setup.sh:349`. This is a distinct omitted entry point from the previously identified `update`/`apply` targets, and lets an unattended worker apply dotfiles (and run bootstrap) despite the operator-only lifecycle policy. **<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Forbid separated verbose recursive rm flags**

When an agent uses `rm -r -v -f build` (or `rm -v -r -f build`), this rule does not match: it requires `-f` immediately after `-r`/`-R`, while the preceding rule only recognizes `-rvf`-style combined tokens. GNU `rm` accepts `-r`, `-f`, and `-v` as independent options ([reference](https://www.gnu.org/software/coreutils/manual/html_node/rm-invocation.html)), so these recursive forced removals receive the normal policy instead of the stated forbidden decision. Despite the earlier combined-form disposition, the final ruleset still has no match for separately tokenized `-v`; add those orderings and inline match tests.

`chezmoi init --one-shot <repo>` does not match this alternative list and therefore falls through to the normal policy, even though chezmoi documents `--one-shot` as equivalent to `--apply` (among other destructive options) and it consequently applies the source state. The [chezmoi update reference](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/commands/update/) documents `--apply` as true by default, so this is a direct operator-only home-state mutation path that bypasses the `chezmoi apply` denial; add an update prefix and a match test.

The [chezmoi edit reference](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/commands/edit/) states that this flag applies the target immediately after editing, so an agent can still mutate a managed home target under the normal policy; add rules and match cases for these forms.

The listed tokens omit `chezmoi init -a=true` and `chezmoi init --one-shot=true`, both of which enable the same boolean apply paths but do not exact-match any prefix here. Chezmoi exposes `-a, --apply` and `--one-shot` as apply-capable flags in its [init reference](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/commands/init/), and its Cobra/pflag parser accepts boolean assignments such as `-f=true` and `--flag=true` ([pflag syntax](https://github.com/spf13/pflag/blob/master/README.md)); add these explicit tokens and tests.

items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Forbid explicit infrastructure destruction**

In a workspace with live Terraform or Kubernetes credentials, `terraform destroy -auto-approve` and `kubectl delete --all` do not match this apply-only rule and therefore fall through to the normal approval policy. Terraform documents that `destroy` deprovisions all managed objects and is an `apply -destroy` alias ([reference](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/destroy)), while Kubernetes documents that `kubectl delete` removes resources, including all selected resources ([reference](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_delete/)); add explicit forbidden prefixes and match tests for these destructive commands.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

items.author: chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]
items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Block direct setup script invocations**

When a worker runs `./setup.sh` from the repository root, no rule matches its initial command, so it receives the normal approval policy even though this documented lifecycle entry point reaches `chezmoi apply` at `setup.sh:349`. Blocking only `make setup` leaves the direct wrapper usable for unattended bootstrap/home-state mutation; add a forbidden prefix (and match test) for the direct setup entry point.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

items.author: chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]
items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Cover grouped force and verbose rm flags**

Fresh evidence beyond the previously covered all-in-one and fully separated forms: `rm -r -fv build` (likewise `-vf` and the corresponding `-R`/reordered forms) is a valid recursive forced removal, but its third token is neither `-f` nor `--force`, so it matches none of these rules and receives the normal policy. Local `rm --help` confirms that `-r` is recursive and `-f` is force; add the grouped two-flag variants and inline match tests.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
items.disposition: not-applicable:`rm -r -fv` is a further spelling of the recursive-force class already covered in combined, split and separated -v orderings; prefix rules enumerate spellings and the header states that rules cover the documented invocation forms only with the sandbox as the backstop (stop rule, revise round 2)

items.author: chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]
items.body:
**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Forbid the clean make target**

`make clean` is unmatched because `clean` is absent from this target union, but its recipe executes `rm -rf docs/reference site` at `Makefile:209`. Since execpolicy evaluates the requested `make clean` command rather than its spawned `rm`, an agent can perform the very recursive forced deletion this policy declares never delegated; add `clean` and an inline match test.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
